issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around war-zone trauma appraisals of injustice/accountability and a threat pattern of hypervigilance, startle, and concentration problems. Self-harm to release overwhelming feelings introduces a distinct affect-regulation strategy that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and sits poorly with the formulation, where Maladaptive Strategies has only a modest reciprocal link with Threat and no links from Negative Appraisals. Given the rest of the profile, a more threat-management strategy would be expected; this item feels clinically out of pattern rather than impossible.

vignette: Three years ago, Jide was deployed to a conflict zone in northern Syria as a field coordinator for an international relief organization. He remembered the morning the supply convoy was ambushed near the border checkpoint: the sudden crack of rifle fire, the acrid smell of burning diesel, and the deafening impact as a mortar struck the lead truck. He spent the next twenty minutes crawling through shattered concrete, trying to shield a wounded medic while his own radio sparked and died. When the gunfire finally stopped, Jide realized he had abandoned the med kits and his team’s communication gear, forced to flee with only his life vest. The aftermath offered no resolution; the contractors who had arranged the route vanished, and no official inquiry was ever opened. For Jide, the event crystallized a quiet, suffocating certainty: what had happened to him was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done to hold anyone accountable. More damaging was the erosion of his own trust; he replayed the moment he had hesitated, convinced he simply could not rely on himself. These judgments took immediate hold, pulling him into a state of relentless physical alarm. The conviction that the perpetrators faced no consequences merged with his belief that he was fundamentally unreliable, keeping his nervous system locked in a constant state of watchfulness. Jide found himself perpetually braced, his shoulders tight and his posture rigid as if expecting another ambush, his nerves frayed to the point where every slamming car door or dropped pen made him jolt violently. The sense that the world remained unaccountable and hostile siphoned his mental energy entirely, leaving his focus fragmented. He would stare at his phone for hours, unable to track a single email thread, his mind constantly fracturing into what-if scenarios as his concentration steadily eroded. The exhaustion of living in that state eventually forced Jide to build walls around his own mind. Because he was constantly scanning for danger and finding it everywhere, he learned to detach himself from the memories entirely, stepping away from the images of the burning truck and the silence that followed. He avoided thinking about the event as a deliberate strategy, telling himself he was just being practical. At his current job as a social media manager in a sunlit, open-plan studio, this avoidance manifested as a rigid routine. Every time he walked into the editing bay or a client conference room, his eyes automatically darted to the exits, mapped sightlines, and catalogued the positions of everyone present. He told his wife, Elena, that he was just being more aware, but the habit of constantly scanning the environment for signs of threat had become an automatic, non-negotiable response. Unfortunately, these very defenses kept the alarm system firing. When Jide successfully detached from the memories or pushed the event out of his thoughts, the suppressed images would inevitably surface in his periphery, interpreted not as fragments but as active warnings that he was still in danger. The act of constantly checking his surroundings never actually verified safety; instead, it trained his body to remain superalert to ordinary stimuli. Each time he scanned a crowded coffee shop or a campaign strategy meeting and found no immediate threat, his nervous system interpreted the absence of danger as a brief respite rather than proof of safety, immediately resetting his baseline for watchfulness. His concentration suffered further because his brain was split between processing analytics and monitoring escape routes, making the startle response sharper with every missed notification or sudden office phone ring. The toll became impossible to ignore six months ago when a live-streamed product launch derailed mid-campaign. Jide had been explaining a branding pivot when a delivery van backfired outside the glass-walled studio. He didn’t just flinch; he froze, his breath shallow, eyes locked on the window until the sound resolved into an ordinary engine. Elena found him later, trembling in the parking garage, insisting he had lost his nerve on air. He knew she was right. He couldn’t track quarterly metrics anymore, nor could he sit through dinner without his posture rigid and his gaze tracing the perimeter of the room. What finally pushed Jide to schedule an intake was the realization that he was spending his days bracing for a war that had ended, while his life quietly unraveled around him. He was afraid the detachment and scanning would become permanent, but he hoped that by understanding how his own defenses were feeding the fear, he might finally step out of the cycle.
